> **The research decision.** When a law, a date, or a cutoff assigned the treatment
> instead of you, decide which comparison you are willing to defend as the world that
> did not happen, and write down the one assumption that makes it stand in. The rule
> is in the documents and the assumption is in your sentence, so no tool gets to
> declare that the comparison it found is the counterfactual.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: which comparison you will defend as the world where the rule never applied.**

> *"You tell me employment fell after the wage law passed. Employment also fell in
> the county next door, which passed nothing. Before I read your effect, tell me what
> you are subtracting, and why that county is the right thing to subtract."*
> — a **state budget analyst**, reading a memo on a minimum-wage increase

A state raises its wage floor on a fixed date. A scholarship goes to
every applicant who scores 70 or higher. A city bans smoking in bars from the first
of the month. Each rule hands you a treated group for free. None of them hands you
the missing world. You still have to pick a comparison: the neighboring state, the
applicants who scored 69, the months before the ban. Pick badly and a regional
recession, a lucky cohort, or a winter flu season wears the policy's name. Pick well
and say why, and a policy question that no one could ever randomize gets a bounded,
defensible causal answer. This chapter gives you three ways to build that
comparison and the check each one owes a skeptical reader.

## The concept

This chapter extends the observational-causal pathway you met earlier in
[Observational Causal Research](../part3-pathways/12-observational-causal-research.qmd).
There, a **natural experiment** was a situation where a force outside anyone's
control decided who got treated. Two of the three designs below, difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity, are declared
in the observational-causal section of the design library in RDSS, with their
estimands and their failure points diagnosed by simulation [@blair2023rdss].

An **assignment rule** is the written procedure that decided which units were
treated and when. Example: a statute that raises the minimum wage in one state on
April 1, or a program manual that funds every applicant scoring 70 or above. You find the rule in primary documents: the law
itself, the agency's notice, the program's scoring sheet. A news story about the
rule is a lead, not the rule. Read it exactly, including the exemptions, the
announcement date, and whether anyone could see the rule coming and act early.

### Difference-in-differences: change against change

**Difference-in-differences** is a design that compares how much the treated group
changed with how much an untreated group changed over the same period. Example:
employment in fast-food restaurants in a state that raised its wage floor fell by
three workers per store, while stores across the border fell by two, so the
difference-in-differences is minus one. Subtracting the neighbor's change removes
whatever hit both places at once, such as a regional downturn or a holiday season.

The quantity this design targets is the **average effect on the treated**, the
average change the policy caused among the units that actually got it, in the
periods after it began. Example: the effect of this raise on these stores in these
quarters, not the effect of every minimum wage everywhere.

One assumption carries the whole design. **Parallel trends** is the assumption that,
without the policy, the treated group's outcome would have moved, on average, by the
same amount as the comparison group's. Example: had the wage law never passed, employment at the
treated stores would have fallen by the same two workers as the stores across the
border. You can never observe that sentence, because the law did pass. You can only make it
plausible.

The tool for making it plausible is the **event study**, a chart of the
treated-minus-comparison gap period by period, before and after the policy, each
measured relative to the last period before it began. The pre-policy estimates are
called **leads**. Example: if the gap was already widening in the four quarters
before the raise, the leads slope, and the comparison state was a poor stand-in from
the start. Leads that slope are a warning you should act on. Leads that sit near
zero are reassuring and nothing more, because a pre-period check can be too
imprecise to see a real divergence, and because trends can part ways exactly when
the policy arrives [@roth2022pretest; @roth2023trending].

Two quieter assumptions ride along. **No anticipation** means the treated units did
not change course before the policy began. Example: if owners cut staff when the law
was announced, months before it took effect, your "before" period already holds part
of the effect. **No spillover** means the policy did not reach the comparison group.
Example: if workers who lost hours crossed the border to take jobs, the comparison
stores changed because of the law too. The closeness that makes a neighbor a good
comparison is what lets a policy leak across the line.

One warning concerns timing. When units adopt a policy on different dates, say
states raising their wage floors in different years, the common shortcut of one
regression with a term for each unit and each period can quietly compare late
adopters with early adopters whose effects are still unfolding, and the weighted
average it returns can even carry the wrong sign. Newer estimators compare each
adopting group only with units not yet treated or never treated, and a review of them is the place
to start before you write that regression [@roth2023trending].

### Regression discontinuity: the effect at the line

**Regression discontinuity** is a design that compares units just above and just
below a cutoff on a score that decides treatment. Example: small firms that scored
70 on a grant application received the grant, firms that scored 69 did not, and a
point of score says little about a firm's prospects. The score is the **running
variable**, the number the rule reads, and the **cutoff** is the value where
treatment switches on. The design estimates the jump in the outcome right at the
line [@lee2010regression].

The estimand is narrow on purpose: the effect for units whose score sits at the
cutoff. Example: what the grant did for firms that scored about 70, not for a firm
that scored 40. The warrant is **continuity**, the
assumption that, without the rule, average outcomes would change smoothly as the
score crosses the line. Here every firm at 70 or above got the grant. If crossing
the line only raised the chance of treatment, say because some winners turned the
grant down, the jump would measure the effect of becoming eligible; recovering the
grant's own effect (a fuzzy discontinuity) is a step to learn with a mentor.

The **bandwidth** is how far from
the cutoff you reach for data. Example: firms scoring 60 to 80 rather than 40 to 100.
A narrow bandwidth compares more similar units but uses fewer of them, so the
interval widens. A wide one is more precise and leans harder on the straight line you
drew. Fix the bandwidth, or the data-driven rule that will choose it, before you see
the estimate, and report the answer at two or three bandwidths. Published work goes
further: it lets a rule pick the bandwidth that best trades bias against noise,
weights applicants more heavily the closer they sit to the line, fits straight lines
or gentle curves near the cutoff rather than one high-order curve across the whole
score range [@gelman2019high], and reports an interval built to survive the bias a
straight line leaves behind [@calonico2014robust]. The `rdrobust` package, written
by the authors of that interval, does all of this. **Sorting** is units
nudging their own score across the line. Example: applicants who learn the cutoff
and rewrite a borderline application. You look for it in a **density check**, a
count of units just below and just above the cutoff; a pile-up on the side the rule
rewards is a warning. And you check **covariate balance at the
cutoff**: traits fixed before the score, such as firm age, should not jump at 70
[@cattaneo2020practical].

### Interrupted time series: one unit, many periods

An **interrupted time series** is a design that follows one unit over many periods
and compares what happened after a policy with the path the earlier periods
projected. Example: monthly hospital admissions for heart attacks in one region,
before and after a smoking ban in bars. The counterfactual is the pre-ban trend,
carried forward. The design is common in public health, where a whole population is
treated at once [@bernal2017interrupted].

Its weak points are easy to name. **Seasonality** is a pattern that repeats every
year, such as winter admission spikes, which can pass for a policy effect if the
policy starts in spring. A **competing event** is anything else that changed on the
same date, such as a new tax on cigarettes, and the series alone cannot tell the two
apart. Months are also not independent pieces of evidence: a busy month tends to
follow a busy month, and an interval that ignores this comes out too narrow. A
**comparison series**, an untreated region or an outcome the policy should not
touch, turns the design into a close cousin of difference-in-differences.

### What the three designs license

On the compass, all three serve a causal question. The crossing license is
identification: an argument, grounded in how the rule assigned treatment, that the
comparison stands in for the missing world. With no further argument, the reach is
the data at hand: the treated units
you observed, in the periods you observed, or the applicants near the cutoff. The
interval still belongs in the answer, because it says how far the estimate could move
if the same units ran through the same periods again with fresh noise. If
those units were drawn by a sampling procedure from a larger list, say a random
sample of every fast-food restaurant in the state, sampling can carry the answer to
that population. Carrying it to another state, another decade, or scores far from
the line is a transported effect, which needs its own argument. And if the
assumption cannot be made plausible, say so: *causal, currently unidentified* is a
legitimate conclusion.

The failure this chapter watches for has a name you already know. **Design mimicry**
is borrowing a design's vocabulary for a comparison that never met its assumption.
Example: calling a plain before-and-after comparison in one state a
"difference-in-differences", or calling any threshold a "discontinuity" when
applicants could see it and aim for it.

An AI partner can find the statute behind a date, fit an event study in seconds, and
list competing events you had not thought of. It is also the fastest route to design
mimicry, because it will run any of these designs on any data you hand it and label
the output with the design's name. It cannot know whether applicants saw the cutoff
coming, or which bandwidth you meant to use before you saw the answer. *AI is your arm and your
research assistant, not your brain*: the rule, the comparison, and the assumption
stay with you.

> **A question that often comes up here:** *"Can't I just test whether the trends
> were parallel and be done?"* You can test whether the leads look flat. You cannot
> test the counterfactual after the policy starts. Report the leads with their
> intervals, say how large a divergence your check could have seen, and keep the
> assumption in your limitations.

## A worked example

Bring this into labor economics. Two neighboring states share a border, a labor
market, and the same weather. State A raises its minimum wage; State B does not. You
survey 200 fast-food restaurants on each side in the quarter before the raise and
again in the quarter after, and you count full-time-equivalent workers. This is the
setting of a well-known study that surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants in New Jersey
and eastern Pennsylvania before and after New Jersey's 1992 increase and compared
their employment changes [@card1994minimum]. The numbers below are constructed for
this example. They do not come from that paper, whose authors found no indication
that the raise reduced employment.

In the constructed world, a regional downturn cuts two workers per store on both
sides of the border, and the raise itself cuts one more, only in State A. A reporter
who looks only at State A sees a drop of almost three workers and blames it all on
the law. That is a before-and-after comparison, and it cannot tell the law from the
downturn. State B is your stand-in for the missing world: its change is your
estimate of what State A would have done without the raise. Subtract it and the
downturn cancels, if and only if the two states would have moved together.

The block below builds that world and computes both numbers. Watch the gap between
the first line and the last.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

n = 200                                   # restaurants on each side of the border
# Constructed world: a regional downturn cuts 2.0 workers EVERYWHERE,
# and the wage raise itself cuts 1.0 more, only in State A.
state = np.repeat(["A (raise)", "B (no raise)"], n)
before = rng.normal(20, 4, size=2 * n)
after = before - 2.0 - 1.0 * (state == "A (raise)") + rng.normal(0, 1.5, size=2 * n)
df = pd.DataFrame({"state": state, "change": after - before})

g = df.groupby("state")["change"].agg(["mean", "var", "size"])
a, b = g.loc["A (raise)"], g.loc["B (no raise)"]
did = a["mean"] - b["mean"]
se = np.sqrt(a["var"] / a["size"] + b["var"] / b["size"])
print(f"true effect of the raise           : {-1.0:+.2f} workers")
print(f"before/after, State A only         : {a['mean']:+.2f}")
print(f"before/after, State B only         : {b['mean']:+.2f}")
print(f"difference-in-differences          : {did:+.2f}  "
      f"(95% interval {did - 1.96*se:+.2f} to {did + 1.96*se:+.2f})")
print("\nthe before/after number blames the raise for the downturn;")
print("State B is what lets you subtract it, IF A would have moved like B")
```

State A's stores changed by -2.92 workers, State B's by -1.95, and the
difference-in-differences is -0.97, with a 95% interval from -1.27 to -0.67. The
true effect we planted was -1.00. Now read that interval with suspicion. It treats
the 400 restaurants as 400 independent pieces of evidence, but the policy varied
between only two states. Anything else that hit State A alone in that quarter, a
plant closing or a bad tourist season, moves every store in A together and lands
inside your estimate. With two states, no formula can separate that from the law, so
the real uncertainty is wider than the printed interval. Say so in the write-up, and
add comparison states or earlier quarters if you can get them.

## A seeded simulation

The left panel shows what an event study can and cannot tell you about parallel
trends. It follows 200 and 200 restaurants for eight quarters, in two worlds with the same true effect of -1.0
worker: one where the states would have moved together, and one where State A was
already losing 0.4 workers per quarter relative to State B before the raise. The
right panel shows a regression discontinuity: 2,000 simulated grant applicants, a
grant at a score of 70, and a true jump of 1.5 jobs a year later. The code also runs a
stress test it does not plot: the same applicants with a differently shaped curve. The
seed makes every run reproduce this exact figure and every printed number.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Event study: 200 stores per state, quarters -4..3, raise at quarter 0.
n, quarters, tau = 200, np.arange(-4, 4), -1.0
def event_study(extra_trend):             # extra_trend < 0: A was ALREADY sliding
    base = rng.normal(20, 4, size=(2 * n, 1))
    shock = rng.normal(0, 0.5, size=quarters.size)       # hits both states
    treated = np.repeat([True, False], n)[:, None]
    y = (base + shock + extra_trend * quarters * treated
         + tau * treated * (quarters >= 0)
         + rng.normal(0, 1.5, size=(2 * n, quarters.size)))
    d = y - y[:, [3]]                                     # change since quarter -1
    est = d[:n].mean(0) - d[n:].mean(0)
    se = np.sqrt(d[:n].var(0, ddof=1) / n + d[n:].var(0, ddof=1) / n)
    change = y[:, 4:].mean(1) - y[:, :4].mean(1)          # after avg minus before avg
    did = change[:n].mean() - change[n:].mean()
    did_se = np.sqrt(change[:n].var(ddof=1) / n + change[n:].var(ddof=1) / n)
    return est, se, did, did_se
par, par_se, did_par, se_par = event_study(0.0)
vio, vio_se, did_vio, se_vio = event_study(-0.4)
for name, est, did, s in (("parallel", par, did_par, se_par),
                          ("sliding ", vio, did_vio, se_vio)):
    print(f"{name}: leads {np.round(est[:3], 2)}, after {np.round(est[4:], 2)}, "
          f"overall {did:+.2f} ({did - 1.96*s:+.2f} to {did + 1.96*s:+.2f})")

# Regression discontinuity: grant at score >= 70, true jump 1.5 jobs.
m, cut, jump = 2000, 70, 1.5
score = rng.uniform(40, 100, m)
x = score - cut
noise = rng.normal(0, 2.0, m)
jobs = 5 + 0.08 * x + 0.0008 * x**2 + jump * (x >= 0) + noise
# Stress test: the same applicants and noise, but an S-shaped curve that climbs
# fastest near the cutoff and levels off at both ends. The true jump is still 1.5.
bent = 5 + 3 * np.tanh(x / 12) + jump * (x >= 0) + noise
def rd(h, y=jobs):                         # local straight lines within h points
    ends, ses = [], []
    for side in (x < 0, x >= 0):
        k = side & (np.abs(x) <= h)
        X = np.column_stack([np.ones(k.sum()), x[k]])
        b = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y[k], rcond=None)[0]
        r = y[k] - X @ b
        ses.append(np.sqrt((r @ r / (k.sum() - 2)) * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[0, 0]))
        ends.append(b)
    return ends[1][0] - ends[0][0], np.hypot(*ses), ends
for h in (5, 10, 20):
    e, s, _ = rd(h)
    print(f"bandwidth {h:2d}: jump {e:.2f} (95% interval {e-1.96*s:.2f} to {e+1.96*s:.2f})")
for h in (5, 10, 20):
    e, s, _ = rd(h, bent)
    print(f"S-curve, bandwidth {h:2d}: jump {e:.2f} ({e-1.96*s:.2f} to {e+1.96*s:.2f})")
print("applicants scoring 65-69.9:", ((x >= -5) & (x < 0)).sum(),
      "| scoring 70-74.9:", ((x >= 0) & (x < 5)).sum())

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.8))
ax1.errorbar(quarters - .12, par, yerr=1.96 * par_se, fmt="o", color="#2a78d6",
             capsize=2, label="parallel trends hold")
ax1.errorbar(quarters + .12, vio, yerr=1.96 * vio_se, fmt="s", color="#eb6834",
             capsize=2, label="treated state already sliding")
ax1.plot([-0.5, 3.4], [tau, tau], color="#333333", ls="--")
ax1.axhline(0, color="#bbbbbb"); ax1.legend(fontsize=8)
edges = np.arange(40, 100.01, 2.5); bins = np.digitize(score, edges) - 1
ax2.scatter((edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2,
            [jobs[bins == i].mean() for i in range(edges.size - 1)], color="#777777")
_, _, (b0, b1) = rd(10)                    # the two local lines at bandwidth 10
xl, xr = np.linspace(-10, 0, 20), np.linspace(0, 10, 20)
ax2.plot(cut + xl, b0[0] + b0[1] * xl, color="#2a78d6")
ax2.plot(cut + xr, b1[0] + b1[1] * xr, color="#2a78d6")
ax2.axvline(cut, color="#333333", ls="--")
plt.show()
```

![Leads that slope before the policy expose a failed comparison, and the grant's
effect shows up as a jump at the cutoff.](../images/sims/natural_experiments.png){fig-alt="Two-panel chart. Left: event-study dot-and-whisker plot over quarters -4 to 3, blue circles for a world where parallel trends hold and orange squares for a world where the treated state was already sliding, with a dashed line at the true effect of -1.0 after the raise. Blue leads sit near zero; orange leads fall from +1.08 at quarter -4 to +0.31 at quarter -2, and orange post-policy estimates keep falling to -2.81 by quarter 3. Right: grey binned means of jobs one year later against application score from 40 to 100, a dashed vertical line at 70, and blue local straight lines within 10 points on each side showing a jump labeled estimated jump 1.36, 95% interval 0.77 to 1.94."}

Read the left panel first. In the blue world, the three leads sit between +0.07 and
+0.14 workers, each with an interval of about plus or minus 0.4 that covers zero.
After the raise, the blue estimates hover around the true -1.0. The overall
difference-in-differences, which compares each store's average over the four
quarters after the raise with the four before, comes out at -1.15 (95% interval
-1.36 to -0.95). In the orange world the leads slope: +1.08 four quarters out, +0.68 three quarters out,
+0.31 two quarters out. State A was already falling behind, so the post-policy
estimates keep sliding to -2.81 by the fourth quarter, and the overall
difference-in-differences reads -2.59 (95% interval -2.80 to -2.38). That interval is
narrow and nowhere near the truth. A sloped trend is not noise, and 400 restaurants
make the wrong number precise rather than right. Notice also the orange lead
closest to the policy: +0.31 with an interval that crosses zero. Someone who checked
only that one quarter would have called the trends parallel.

Now the right panel. At a bandwidth of 10 points the estimated jump is 1.36 jobs
(95% interval 0.77 to 1.94), against a true 1.5. At 5 points it is 1.24 (0.44 to
2.05), wider because fewer applicants sit that close to the line. At 20 points it is
1.23 (0.80 to 1.66), tighter because it uses more applicants. The three agree on the
sign and roughly on the size. You report all three, led by the bandwidth you fixed in
advance. Do not read the 20-point shortfall as the price of a straight line. Here
the curve bends the same way on both sides of 70, so on average the two lines miss
the cutoff by the same amount and the misses cancel. The gap from 1.5 is noise.

The stress test shows when a wide window does cost you. Its curve is S-shaped: jobs
climb fastest for scores near 70 and level off at both ends. The applicants, the noise,
and the true jump of 1.5 are unchanged. At 5 points the estimate is 1.27 (0.46 to
2.08), and at 10 points 1.54 (0.95 to 2.12). At 20 points it is 2.08 (1.65 to 2.51), an
interval that no longer contains the truth. The straight lines cut across the bend, and
the interval, which counts only noise, cannot see the bias. The rise from 5 to 20 points
is the warning sign, which is why you report several bandwidths and a second curve
shape. Treat these intervals as a teaching device; a real discontinuity
reports the bias-aware interval described earlier.

The density check counts 187 applicants just below the cutoff and
162 just above. A gap of that size, about 1.3 standard errors, turns up often by
chance, and it runs the opposite way to a pile-up on the treated side. It lowers
your concern about sorting without settling it, because a density check can only see
sorting large enough to leave a mark in the counts. Comparing raw counts works here
only because the simulated scores are spread evenly; with real scores, whose density
slopes, a formal density test fits that slope on each side of the line
[@cattaneo2020practical]. In the companion notebook, change
the `-0.4` to `-0.1` and watch the orange leads crowd back toward zero while the
post-policy estimates stay biased.

## Where these designs show up

In political science, close elections are the classic discontinuity. A candidate who
wins by a fraction of a point is, on average, much like one who loses by a fraction
of a point, so comparing the parties that barely won with those that barely lost
estimates what holding a seat does for a party's chances next time
[@lee2008randomized]. The estimand is the effect for races decided by a whisker, not
for landslides. The checks still bind here. In postwar U.S. House races, bare winners
turned out to differ from bare losers before the vote, in money, experience, and
incumbency, which is exactly what a covariate-balance check at the cutoff exists to
catch [@caughey2011elections].

In business, a retailer that changes its return policy in one region on a fixed date
invites a difference-in-differences against regions that kept the old policy. The threat is that the retailer picked the
region because its sales were already slipping, the sloped lead an event study
exists to catch.

In public health, the smoking-ban series above grows more convincing once it gains a
comparison series from an untreated region [@bernal2017interrupted]. In ecology, a
fishing ban on some reefs from a fixed date sets up the same change-against-change
comparison with reefs that stayed open. For a readable treatment of
difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity, with code, see Cunningham's
textbook, free to read online [@cunningham2021mixtape].

## An AI failure case

You paste your event-study table into a chatbot and ask whether your
difference-in-differences is valid. It answers with a confident, well-formatted yes:
"None of the pre-treatment coefficients is statistically significant, so the
parallel trends assumption holds and the estimate can be interpreted causally." This
is two named failures at once. It is a **plausible-but-wrong method**, treating a
failure to detect a pre-trend as proof that none exists, and it shows **missing
uncertainty**, reporting a verdict with no word about how large a divergence your
leads could have seen. A quiet lead is not a parallel trend. You catch it by plotting
all the leads with their intervals, asking how large a pre-trend the check could have
missed, and reading the slope across quarters rather than any one lead's verdict. A
sensitivity analysis can go one step further and ask how far your post-policy estimate
moves if the trend kept diverging after the policy by up to a multiple of the largest
divergence the leads show, a multiple you choose and report [@rambachan2023more]. Then you rewrite the
sentence: the leads show no clear divergence at the precision the sample allows, and
the post-policy comparison still rests on the untestable assumption that the states
would have moved together. Log why.

This further route is where that rule becomes a comparison you can defend in
writing, or an honest statement that it cannot be one yet.*

before you accept it.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. You decide **what the assignment rule actually was**, read
from the primary document, including when it was announced and who could see it
coming. You decide **which comparison stands in for the world without the rule**,
and you write the assumption that lets it. And you decide **whether the checks leave
that assumption plausible enough to carry *because***, or whether your answer is
causal, currently unidentified. A tool can fit the model, draw the plot, and find
papers. The counterfactual you defend carries your name.
:::

1. Quote the assignment rule from its primary document. Write the exact sentence of
   the law, manual, or policy that decided treatment, with its source, its
   effective date, and its announcement date. Then write which of the three designs
   it fits: a date with an untreated comparison group (difference-in-differences), a
   cutoff on a score (regression discontinuity), or one population treated at once
   (interrupted time series).

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a policy research librarian. I am studying [the policy] in [place] around
   [date]. Find the primary documents that set the rule: the statute or regulation,
   the agency notice, and any published scoring or eligibility sheet. For each, give
   the issuing body, the document title, the date, and where I can retrieve it. Only
   include documents you are confident exist; mark anything uncertain.
   ```

   After running, verify: open every document yourself and find the sentence that
   assigns treatment; cut any item you cannot retrieve. Counters **confident
   fabrication** (an invented statute number arrives as confidently as a real one).
2. Write your Research Contract lines for this route. Your question, as a treatment
   and an outcome. Your estimand, in one sentence that names whose effect, over which
   periods, or at which cutoff. Your data strategy: the units, the periods or score
   range, and the comparison group. Your answer strategy: the difference you will
   compute and the interval you will report, including how that interval accounts
   for the policy changing place by place rather than store by store. Your warrant:
   parallel trends, continuity at the cutoff, or a stable pre-trend, written in
   plain words a skeptic could argue with.
3. Name the threat most likely to break your warrant, and the check you will run.
   For difference-in-differences, an event study with every lead shown, and a note on
   whether units adopted on different dates. For a discontinuity, the density check,
   covariate balance at the cutoff, and the estimate at two or three bandwidths you
   fix before looking, with a bias-aware interval and a second curve shape. For an interrupted
   time series, seasonality and the competing events of that same date, plus a
   comparison series.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a hostile labor economist. Here is my design: [paste rule, comparison,
   outcome, periods]. List every event, trend, or behavior that could move my
   treated group differently from my comparison group around [date], in a table with
   the threat, the direction it would push my estimate, and the data I could use to
   check it. Then name the single threat you think I am most likely to miss.
   ```

   After running, verify: compare the table with the threat you wrote first, and for
   each row find one real source that says the event happened when and where the
   tool says. Counters **illusion of completeness** (a tidy table that omits the one
   competing event that shares your date).
4. Run a falsification test and say in advance what it would look like if your
   design were in trouble. Move the policy date to an earlier year when nothing
   happened, using only data from before the real policy. Or move the cutoff to a
   score where nothing changes, using only applicants on one side of the real cutoff
   so its jump cannot leak in. Or use an outcome the policy should not touch. A placebo estimate far from zero is a warning. One near zero
   lowers your concern about that specific threat, as far as the test was sensitive
   to it, and leaves the rest of the warrant where it was.

   *When you are ready to delegate this step:*

   ```text
   Act as a skeptical referee. Here is my design and the choices I fixed BEFORE
   seeing the estimate: [paste rule, comparison, outcome, periods or bandwidth].
   Propose three placebo tests for it: a fake policy date, a fake cutoff, or an
   outcome the policy should not touch. For each, tell me what result would worry
   me and roughly how large an effect the test could detect with my sample. Do not
   suggest changing my bandwidth, comparison group, or window to improve my main
   result.
   ```

   After running, verify: open the documents again and confirm that no real rule
   changed at each fake date or cutoff, then run every placebo yourself and check
   that any number the tool quotes appears in your own output. If it slips in a new
   bandwidth or window that makes the main result significant, reject it and note it
   in your ledger. Counters **sycophantic agreement** (a helper that finds the result
   you seemed to want).
5. Write the boundary sentence. State what your estimate describes, for whom, and
   over which periods or at which cutoff, with its interval, and name the one
   assumption a reader must accept for the word *because* to stand. If your checks
   left the assumption implausible, write the causal-language boundary instead: what
   the comparison shows, and the *because* you are declining to claim.
6. Log the step in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one output with a
   named method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd). A
   **falsification test** is the natural check for this route: the placebo date,
   placebo cutoff, or untouched outcome from step 4. **Simulation** is the strong
   second check: build a small world in which your comparison group was already
   drifting, as the orange world above was, and see whether your event study would
   have shown it. An AI reviewer may run the checks with you; the decision to accept
   or reject stays yours.
